text: 7 System Evaluation We evaluate the design and implementation of Afore by answering the following research questions: • (RQ1) How does Afore compare against state-of-the-art baselines in output throughput and P95 inter-token latency? • (RQ2) How efficient and effective is Afore ’s scheduling algorithm in practice? • (RQ3) How much does each system design contribute to Afore ’s performance gains? • (RQ4) How effectively does AFD pipeline overlap hide expert-migration overhead? 7.1 Experimental Setup Hardware environment. We conduct all experiments on a cluster of two machines, each equipped with eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Within each node, the eight GPUs are interconnected through NVLink and NVSwitch, providing a peak unidirectional bandwidth of 300 GB/s per GPU. For inter-node communication, each node provides eight RDMA-enabled bonded network interfaces with 50 GB/s of unidirectional bandwidth per bond. Models and workloads. We evaluate Afore on a 110B-parameter MoE model (i.e., GLM-4.5-Air ), served under a PD+AFD deployment. We construct four representative serving workloads from ShareGPT [ 31 ] , FineWeb [ 19 ] , CodeForces [ 20 ] , and GSM8K [ 3 ] . These workloads are diverse, covering conversational requests, document-style inputs, code-generation tasks, and mathematical-reasoning queries, respectively. We replay the traces to generate dynamic serving workloads whose expert-token distributions shift over time. Evaluation metrics. We report standard LLM serving metrics. We measure end-to-end output throughput in tokens per second and P95 inter-token latency (ITL), which captures the tail latency of decode-token generation. For migration-specific analysis, we report raw migration cost and exposed migration cost on the target microbatch’s critical path. Baselines. We compare Afore against representative expert-placement and reconfiguration policies. For a fair comparison, we implement all baselines inside the same AFD serving runtime and run them with the same model, hardware, GPU allocation, batching policy, and workloads: • Static , a fixed-placement baseline that evenly assigns experts to FFN workers at initialization and never changes the placement during serving. • EPLB [ 6 ] , a statistics-based reconfiguration policy that periodically rebalances expert placement using load statistics collected over a past profiling window. • HarMoEny [ 7 ] , a reactive load-balancing policy that redistributes tokens and creates redundant expert replicas based on the routing demand observed at runtime. • Lina [ 16 ] , a prediction-based reconfiguration policy that predicts upcoming hot experts from recent expert selection patterns and replicates them in advance. • Libra [ 30 ] , a prediction-based reconfiguration policy that prefetches expert replicas based on predicted next-layer top- k k activations and redistributes tokens according to the actual routing demand. We further evaluate ablated versions of Afore in § 7.4 to isolate the contributions of target-demand visibility and pipeline-overlapped migration. Figure 8 : Upper: Output throughput across four workloads. Lower: P95 inter-token latency under the same workloads. 7.2 End-to-end Performance (RQ1) Figure 8 compares Afore with the baselines across the four workloads. Afore achieves the highest output throughput and the lowest P95 ITL on all workloads. Compared with the strongest competing baseline for each workload, Afore improves throughput by 10.1–17.6% and reduces P95 ITL by 7.1–9.5%. The improvement comes from two effects. First , temporal reconfiguration reduces FFN-side stragglers by adapting expert placement to the routing demand that is about to enter the FFN stage. Second , Afore overlaps expert migration with the AFD pipeline, avoiding the critical-path migration cost that limits more reactive policies. As a result, Afore improves both throughput and tail token latency. The gains persist across workloads, i.e., conversational ( ShareGPT ), document-style ( FineWeb ), coding ( CodeForces ), and mathematical-reasoning ( GSM8K ) workloads. Despite their different request characteristics and routing patterns, Afore consistently improves the MoE serving efficiency, showing that temporal expert reconfiguration is robust across diverse workload types. 7.3 Scheduler Overhead and Solution Quality (RQ2) Evaluation configuration. We evaluate whether Afore ’s scheduler is efficient enough to run at microbatch granularity while producing high-quality plans. We replay routing traces from the four workloads under EP degrees 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, sampling the same 200 steady-state targets (50 per workload) at each EP degree. For scheduling overhead, we report the median scheduler core latency across the sampled targets. For solution quality, we compare Afore ’s maximum worker tile load with the optimum under the same placement and copy constraints. Optimality is certified by matching the average tile-load lower bound or by exact optimization under the same constraints. We report the relative gap between Afore ’s maximum worker tile load and the optimum. Figure 9 : Median scheduler core latency of Afore across EP degrees. Table 2 : Scheduler solution quality. Gaps are relative to the optimum. EP 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 Optimal / 200 196 197 200 200 200 200 200 Mean gap (%) 0.04 0.03 0 0 0 0 0 Max gap (%) 3.60 1.89 0 0 0 0 0 Scheduling overhead. As shown in Figure 9 , Afore ’s scheduler adds only sub-millisecond planning overhead across all tested EP degrees. Its median latency is 8.23 μ \mu s at EP=2 and remains 245.81 μ \mu s even at EP=128. This low planning cost makes the scheduler suitable for microbatch-level reconfiguration as the number of workers increases. Solution quality. Table 2 compares Afore ’s greedy scheduler with the certified optimum in maximum worker tile load. At EP=2 and EP=4, the mean optimality gap is at most 0.04%, with a worst-case gap of 3.60% across the two settings. At every tested EP degree from 8 to 128, Afore achieves the optimum on all 200 targets. Overall, it achieves the optimal maximum worker tile load on 99.5% of the 1,400 targets. These results show that Afore ’s scheduler provides an effective trade-off for online serving: it combines the low latency needed for frequent reconfiguration with near-optimal load balance, even at high EP degrees. 7.4 Component-wise Ablation (RQ3) Evaluation configuration. We isolate the effects of demand prefetching and migration overlap. Full Afore enables both mechanisms. w/o Prefetch replaces the target microbatch’s demand with the previous step’s demand at the same layer and microbatch position, while retaining the same scheduler and migration mechanism. w/o Overlap retains demand prefetching and the same scheduler, but places expert migration on the critical path. Static disables runtime reconfiguration and serves as a fixed-placement reference. All configurations use the same model, workload, resource allocation, and batching policy. End-to-end contribution. Figure 10 reports output throughput and P95 inter-token latency across the four workloads. Compared with Static, full Afore improves throughput by 26.0–34.1% (29.8% on average) and reduces P95 ITL by 16.7–19.6% (18.2% on average). The combined design consistently improves serving performance over fixed expert placement. Demand prefetching. Disabling demand prefetching reduces throughput by 12.4–17.9% and increases P95 ITL by 6.3–10.5% relative to full Afore . Without the target microbatch’s routing demand, the scheduler acts on historical observations and may optimize for a load distribution that has already changed. The degradation across workloads illustrates the value of timely routing information for expert reconfiguration. Table 3 : Ablation study configurations. Configuration Reconfig. Lower: P95 inter-token latency under the same configurations. Migration overlap. Without pipeline overlap, throughput drops by 15.2–21.3%, while P95 ITL rises by 12.2–16.0%. Delaying expert copies exposes their latency on the target microbatch’s critical path, even though the scheduler still uses its actual routing demand. Therefore, demand prefetching and migration overlap play complementary roles: prefetching improves which placement is selected, while overlap reduces the cost of installing that placement. 7.5 Migration Hiding Effectiveness (RQ4) Evaluation configuration. We measure the raw migration cost from copy submission to completion and the exposed migration cost as the remaining wait for copies when the target microbatch needs them. Their difference is the migration time hidden by pipeline overlap. We also measure the lookahead window from copy submission to the target microbatch’s first use of the replicas. Migration cost. The left panel of Figure 11 compares raw migration cost with the lookahead window across the four workloads. Mean raw migration cost ranges from 0.453–0.495 ms, compared with a mean lookahead window of 2.008–2.119 ms. All 324 sampled targets complete their required copies before use, yielding zero exposed migration cost. Thus, pipeline overlap fully hides the migration time in these samples and keeps it off the target microbatch’s critical path. Figure 11 : Left: Raw migration cost D D versus lookahead window W W . Right: CDF of time remaining before use (minimum across ranks per target). Time remaining before use. The right panel of Figure 11 reports the time between copy completion and first use, taking the minimum across participating ranks for each target. The median remaining time ranges from 1.459–1.668 ms across workloads, with a minimum of 0.447 ms. This remaining window allows additional migration delay to be absorbed before it becomes exposed on the target microbatch’s critical path. 8 Conclusion In this paper, we presented Afore , a timely expert reconfig
